newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. informs allies of NATO enlargement wish.
newsitem.headline: U.S. informs allies of NATO enlargement wish.

text.p: The U.S. on Thursday informed NATO it wanted to invite only Poland, the Czech Republic, and Hungary to join the alliance at a summit next month, rejecting pressure from France and others for a broader expansion.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen told fellow NATO defence ministers meeting in Brussels of Washington's key decision to limit enlargement to three former communist enemies and not include Slovenia and Romania.
"The announcement by Secretary Cohen was pretty significant and will have a big effect on those who are here," British Defence Minister George Robertson told reporters.
The United States is the most powerful member of NATO, the defence organisation created to defend the West from an attack from the now-defunct Soviet Union which never happened.

All NATO members must approve any enlargement agreed by Western leaders at a July 8-9 summit in Madrid. But Washington's decision is certain to carry most weight despite a push by France and several other countries to admit five new members.
A NATO source at the meeting said the announcement clearly took some other members by surprise.

Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta, whose country favours both Romania's and Slovenia's admission, said he did not agree with Washington's decision and would try to persuade the NATO partners to broaden the invitation.

"I don't agree on this solution. I believe the problems in Europe have a strategic and political aspect... in particular it is quite important to have a balanced distribution of new members," he told reporters.
The White House, concerned that alliance expansion could cost billions of dollars, announced in Washington earlier that the U.S. position was firm and unlikely to be overridden.
France and the supporters of a broader expansion argued that tiny Slovenia and Romania needed to be included in order to maintain a balance within NATO between its northern and southern flanks.

Cohen earlier told reporters that not only cost and military readiness argued against broad expansion, but that there was deep dissension within the U.S. Senate, which must approve the process, and NATO members themselves.
The White House and Cohen said more countries should be invited to join the alliance at a later date, but that Slovenia and Romania needed more time to meet the basic requirements for membership.

"In the view of the United States they will profit by having more time to fully develop their capacities within the parameters of the Partnership for Peace programme," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.
Former Warsaw Pact foes Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, which were left to Josef Stalin's "sphere of influence" at the end of World War Two, have met NATO's basic conditions for membership.
These are respect for human rights and democracy, the establishment of a market economy, and democratic control of the armed forces.
All three countries have also made strenuous efforts to modernise their armed forces in line with NATO standards.
